threads_text: Claude Code now steers away from recreating a specific existing game, even if you rename it. Anthropic says original games and genre games still work. Fair protection for game studios, or a rule that will catch fan projects too?
caption:
Anthropic added a rule to Claude Code that steers it away from recreating a specific existing game, even under a new name.
Original games, genre games and games from your own designs are still fine, an Anthropic staffer said.
It follows a wave of AI-made copies and ports of existing games.

Should AI coding tools refuse to clone games?

paragraphs.text: Anthropic has added an instruction to its Claude Code agent that steers the model away from recreating existing video games, Game Developer reported on October 30, 2026. The rule tells Claude not to build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if the user renames it or calls it original.

The same instruction says Claude should still build original games, games in a genre and games based on the user's own designs and assets. According to MadRobot, that means a new platformer or roguelike is fine, while a renamed copy of a well known game is not.

An X user who posts as Chasm spotted the change and said it was pushed around October 27 under a server flag named tengu_heron_brook, with no setting to switch it off. MadRobot reported that the text appears in Claude Code version 2.1.314, published to npm early on October 30, that it was not in version 2.1.312, and that it does not appear in Anthropic's public changelog.

Anthropic confirmed the update to Game Developer. Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, wrote on X that the company added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game. He said original, genre and own asset games are meant to keep working and that Anthropic will continue to iterate.

MadRobot noted that the rule is an instruction to the model rather than a hard technical block, so how strictly Claude follows it may depend on the request. The setting is tied to Claude Opus 5.5, which means users on other models may not receive it.
A wave of AI made copies

The change follows months of AI assisted game remakes. Kotaku reported on October 15 that the release of Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22 was followed by a wave of vibe coded projects, including web browser ports of well known games, and that GitHub has received many DMCA takedown notices from game publishers related to vibe coding.

Game Developer tied the rule to developer fears about fast follow clones, citing a studio that canceled a public playtest and Valve addressing concerns about AI cloning on Steam. MadRobot reported that some indie developers are holding back public demos because AI tools can copy a game within days. Anthropic is also facing copyright lawsuits over Claude, including one filed this month by the owners of 274 Elvis Presley songs.

The instruction draws a line that copyright law already tends to draw: game ideas and genres are hard to protect, while names, characters, art and code are protected. By putting that line into the agent's prompt, Anthropic is trying to keep Claude Code on the safe side without blocking the large number of people who use it to build their own games. Because Claude has no way to verify who owns a design or asset, the rule relies on how the model reads each request.
Watch whether other AI coding tools adopt similar rules, and whether Anthropic changes the wording after feedback from developers who build mods, fan projects and remakes of abandoned games.
